plan: Ten new items checked against the bank by key word and passage text: spare and conspicuous WIC, mid-sentence however, future perfect, 'ultimately', rarity synthesis, lichen moisture inference, two-part data claim (hard), retired-driver inference, 'whose'.

passages.title: Spare prose
passages.text: The essayist's prose is notably ______: she rarely uses a word that the sentence could do without, and many of her paragraphs consist of a single short sentence.

passages.title: Warning colors
passages.text: Many poisonous animals display ______ coloring, such as bright orange or yellow bands, which makes them easy for predators to notice and, after one unpleasant encounter, to avoid.

passages.title: Reef survey
passages.text: Most of the coral colonies in the survey area had recovered within five years of the bleaching event. The colonies on the reef's outer edge, ______ showed almost no recovery, possibly because warmer currents reached them first.

passages.title: Probe journey
passages.text: A space probe launched in 2023 is expected to reach Jupiter in 2031. By the time it arrives, the probe ______ more than three billion kilometers, using the gravity of Earth and Venus to gain speed along the way.

passages.title: Ceramic choice
passages.text: For the heat shield, the engineers tested more than forty materials, including several metals, carbon composites, and ceramics, under conditions that simulated reentry into the atmosphere. ______ they chose a ceramic tile that was slightly heavier than the best composite but far less likely to crack.

passages.title: Fossil site notes
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 2019, a team of paleontologists excavated a site in Montana.
• They found the nearly complete skeleton of a small horned dinosaur.
• The skeleton was preserved in fine river sediment.
• Nearly complete skeletons of horned dinosaurs are rare.

passages.title: Mist and lichen
passages.text: In a forest, researchers found that a certain lichen grows mostly on the north sides of tree trunks, where the bark stays damp longest. Near a large waterfall in the same forest, however, where spray keeps every surface wet, the lichen grows on all sides of the trunks. These observations suggest that ______

passages.title: Formats and genres
passages.text:
A library surveyed members about how many days they took, on average, to finish a book in print or as an audiobook.
Genre | Print (days) | Audiobook (days)
Novels | 9 | 6
Biography | 12 | 8
Poetry | 5 | 4.5
A librarian claims that audiobook listeners finished books faster than print readers in every genre, but that the difference was smallest for poetry.

passages.title: The early route
passages.text:
The following text is from a short story.
For thirty-one years, Mr. Okafor had driven the number 9 bus, and for thirty-one years his alarm had rung at 4:30. He had been retired for a month now. Every morning he still woke at 4:29, a minute before the alarm he no longer set, and walked to the corner in time to watch the number 9 pull away without him.

passages.title: The cast list
passages.text: Among the actors who auditioned for the role, the director chose Lena Ortiz, ______ performance in a small regional production had impressed critics the year before.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: she rarely uses a word that the sentence could do without
candidates.explanation: Prose with no unnecessary words and very short paragraphs is lean and economical: "spare."

B.rationale: "Ornate" means elaborately decorated, the opposite of prose without extra words.

C.rationale: "Digressive" means wandering from the subject; nothing suggests the essays wander.

D.rationale: "Effusive" means gushing or unrestrained, which does not fit prose with no unnecessary words.

hints: What do the details after the colon say about the writing?
candidates.remember: Use the colon's explanation to define the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: which makes them easy for predators to notice
candidates.explanation: Coloring that is bright and easy to notice is "conspicuous."

A.rationale: "Drab" means dull, the opposite of bright bands.

B.rationale: "Subtle" means hard to notice; the coloring is meant to be easy to notice.

D.rationale: "Variable" means changing; the text describes coloring that stands out, not coloring that changes.

hints: What effect does the coloring have on predators?
candidates.remember: Match the word to the effect the text describes.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: The colonies on the reef's outer edge,
candidates.explanation: "However" interrupts the clause between the subject and the verb, so it is set off by a pair of commas; the first comma is already in place.

A.rationale: "However" interrupts the sentence and must be set off by a comma on both sides.

C.rationale: A semicolon would separate the subject "The colonies on the reef's outer edge" from its verb.

D.rationale: A semicolon after "however" would separate the subject from its verb "showed."

hints: Where are the subject and the verb of the second sentence?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate choices that separate the subject from its verb.

candidates.remember: An interrupting "however" takes commas on both sides.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: "By the time it arrives" refers to a future moment, and the travel will be finished by then, so the future perfect "will have traveled" is correct.

A.rationale: The past perfect places the travel before a past moment, but the arrival is in the future.

B.rationale: The present perfect does not fit travel completed by a future arrival.

C.rationale: The simple present does not show that the travel will be complete by the arrival.

hints: Is the arrival in the past or the future?

strategy.explanation: Match the tense to a completed action before a future point.

candidates.remember: "By the time" + a future event calls for "will have."

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: the engineers tested more than forty materials
candidates.explanation: After describing extensive testing, the text gives the final decision. "Ultimately" signals the end result of a process.

B.rationale: The engineers' final choice is not an example of the testing; it is its outcome.

C.rationale: The choice is the result of the testing, not something similar to it.

D.rationale: Nothing is being replaced; the choice concludes the testing process.

hints: How is the second sentence related to the long testing process?
candidates.remember: Use "ultimately" for the final outcome of a process.

candidates.stem: The student wants to emphasize why the discovery was unusual. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: In 2019, paleontologists excavated a site in Montana that contained a small dinosaur.
choices.B: The skeleton found in Montana had been preserved in fine river sediment.
choices.C: The team found a nearly complete skeleton of a horned dinosaur, a rare kind of find.
choices.D: A team of paleontologists working in Montana in 2019 found a horned dinosaur.

candidates.evidence: Nearly complete skeletons of horned dinosaurs are rare.
candidates.explanation: The find was unusual because nearly complete horned-dinosaur skeletons are rare. Only C states both the completeness and the rarity.

A.rationale: This gives the time and place but not what made the find unusual.

B.rationale: This explains how the skeleton was preserved, not why the find was unusual.

D.rationale: This omits that the skeleton was nearly complete, which is what made it rare.

hints: What made the find unusual, according to the notes?

strategy.explanation: Look for the choice that includes the rarity.

candidates.remember: Match the choice to the specific emphasis in the goal.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the lichen cannot survive on any of the trees that grow far from the waterfall.
choices.B: sunlight is more important to the lichen than moisture is.
choices.C: the lichen grows faster near the waterfall than it does anywhere else in the forest.
choices.D: moisture, not the direction a surface faces, mainly limits where the lichen grows.

candidates.evidence: where spray keeps every surface wet, the lichen grows on all sides
candidates.explanation: The lichen favors the damp north side in the forest, but where every side is wet it grows everywhere. Moisture, not direction, explains the pattern.

A.rationale: The lichen grows in the rest of the forest too, on the damp north sides.

B.rationale: Where moisture is everywhere, direction (and so sunlight) stops mattering, which points to moisture.

C.rationale: The text describes where the lichen grows, not how fast.

hints: What changes near the waterfall, and what happens to the lichen?

strategy.explanation: Compare the two settings and find the variable that matters.

candidates.remember: When one condition is removed and the pattern disappears, that condition was the cause.

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the librarian's claim?

choices.A: Biography took the longest in both formats: 12 days in print and 8 days as an audiobook.
choices.B: Audiobooks were faster in every genre, by 3 days for novels, 4 for biography and only 0.5 for poetry.
choices.C: Poetry took 5 days in print and 4.5 days as an audiobook, the shortest times in the table.
choices.D: Novels took 9 days in print but only 6 days as an audiobook, a difference of 3 days.

candidates.evidence: the difference was smallest for poetry
candidates.explanation: The claim has two parts: audiobooks were faster in every genre, and the gap was smallest for poetry. Only B gives all three differences and shows poetry's is the smallest.

A.rationale: This compares genres, not the size of the format difference.

C.rationale: This shows poetry was fastest overall, not that its format difference was smallest compared with the other genres.

D.rationale: This covers only one genre and says nothing about poetry.

hints: The claim has two parts. Which choice addresses both?

strategy.explanation: Split the claim, then check each choice against both parts.

candidates.remember: Evidence for a comparison across groups must include every group compared.

author_checklist.hardness: Choice C states true poetry figures and that they are the smallest times, which looks like 'smallest for poetry' but measures the wrong thing; students must notice the claim is about differences.

candidates.stem: Based on the text, what can most reasonably be inferred about Mr. Okafor?

choices.A: His long-established routine continues to shape his days even though his job has ended.
choices.B: He regrets retiring and plans to return to work as a bus driver.
choices.C: He walks to the corner each morning because he still has to catch the bus to work.
choices.D: He has trouble sleeping because his alarm still rings every morning.

candidates.evidence: a minute before the alarm he no longer set
candidates.explanation: Waking before an alarm he no longer sets and walking to watch his old bus show that decades of routine still govern his mornings.

B.rationale: Nothing in the text mentions regret or plans to return.

C.rationale: He is retired and watches the bus leave without him.

D.rationale: He no longer sets the alarm.

hints: What does he still do, and why is that notable?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate choices contradicted by the details.

candidates.remember: Infer from what a character does, not from what the text never says.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: The clause describes Ortiz's performance, so the possessive relative pronoun "whose" is needed.

A.rationale: "Who's" means "who is," which does not fit before "performance."

B.rationale: "Who" cannot show possession; the performance belongs to Ortiz.

D.rationale: "Her" would create a comma splice, joining two independent clauses with only a comma.

hints: Does the blank need to show that the performance belongs to Ortiz?

strategy.explanation: Test "who is performance" and check for a comma splice.
